summary:
GeoMoon is an open, web-based scientific platform that joins real NASA lunar terrain, spacecraft parameters and flight physics to plan and simulate Moon landings.

Problem: future Moon colonies will need reliable transport and landings that depend on real terrain (slopes, roughness, craters) and on the specific spacecraft (mass, thrust, fuel). No accessible tool connects them.

Solution: (1) an interactive 3D globe built from real NASA elevation data, with slope, roughness and hazard maps and ranked candidate landing sites; (2) a landing simulator where users define their own vehicle and fly a descent over the real terrain; (3) an Earth-Moon orbital simulator with gravity of Earth, Moon and Sun, an automatic mission planner (trans-lunar burn, lunar orbit capture, guided descent), manual engine control, 2D/3D views, live telemetry and graphs.

Data: NASA LRO LOLA, product LDEM_16 (about 1.9 km per pixel), from the PDS Geosciences Node. Nothing is invented: missing data is reported, synthetic terrain is always labelled.

Method: DOP853 numerical integration, Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Lambert solution refined by numerical shooting. Reference mission: about 3.2 km/s to leave Earth orbit, 1 km/s for capture, touchdown at about 1 m/s.

Quality: 197 backend tests, 82 interface tests, 60 browser checks. GeoMoon is a research prototype, not flight software, and never calls a landing “safe”.

details:
Project title

GeoMoon: Lunar Landing Intelligence

Short summary (one-liner)

A scientific web platform that analyzes real NASA lunar terrain, plans Earth–Moon trajectories and simulates landings for a user-defined spacecraft.

Project details (full description)

The problem. As humanity prepares to settle the Moon, safe transport and landing will depend on two things at once: the real terrain at the landing site (slopes, roughness, craters) and the capabilities of the specific spacecraft (mass, thrust, fuel). Today these are handled by separate, specialized tools; there is no accessible product that connects terrain, vehicle and trajectory in one place.

Our solution. GeoMoon is an open, web-based platform that joins them:

  • Terrain analysis. An interactive 3D globe of the Moon built from real NASA elevation data. For any region it computes slope, roughness, relief and hazard maps and ranks candidate landing sites, with an explanation for each result.
  • Spacecraft and landing simulation. Users define their own vehicle (dry mass, fuel, thrust, specific impulse). The simulator flies a powered descent over the real terrain, detects surface contact and evaluates the surface, the trajectory and the vehicle separately.
  • Orbital flight simulator. An Earth–Moon simulator with gravity of Earth, Moon and Sun, a mission planner (trans-lunar burn, lunar orbit capture, guided descent), manual engine control, a synchronized 2D map and 3D scene, a mission-control dashboard with live telemetry and nine graphs, and the ability to place the vehicle anywhere.

How it works.

  1. NASA terrain data is imported and verified against known reference points (for example, the Apollo 11 site at about −1.9 km and the South Pole–Aitken basin floor at about −9 km).
  2. The user selects a site on the globe or in the orbital simulator and defines the spacecraft and the mission.
  3. The server integrates the equations of motion (gravity of Earth, Moon and Sun plus engine thrust) with the 8th-order DOP853 method with error control. Fuel consumption follows the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation. Moon and Sun positions are time-dependent.
  4. The planner uses a Lambert solution as a first guess and refines it by numerical shooting on the full model. In our reference run, leaving Earth orbit needs about 3.2 km/s, lunar orbit capture about 1 km/s, and the guided descent touches down at about 1 m/s.
  5. Results are shown on the 2D map, the 3D scene, telemetry, graphs and a mission report.

Honest limitations. GeoMoon is a research and educational prototype, not flight software. It never labels a landing “safe”: results only mean that assessed limits are or are not exceeded. If the map resolution is coarser than the landing footprint, the surface is reported as “not assessed” rather than guessed. The Moon ephemeris is an analytical low-precision model (about 0.3°), maneuvers are impulsive approximations, and lunar gravity is a point mass.

Quality. 197 automated backend tests (physics invariants, ephemeris checks, rocket equation, collisions, API consistency), 82 interface tests and 60 end-to-end browser checks.

Next steps. Higher-resolution terrain around candidate sites, NASA JPL ephemerides, non-uniform lunar gravity, spacecraft attitude and guidance during landing, and comparing vehicles and scenarios for colony logistics.

NASA data and resources used

  • LRO LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter), Gridded Data Record, product LDEM_16: global lunar digital elevation model, about 1.9 km per pixel (5760 × 2880). Dataset LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0, NASA PDS Geosciences Node: https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/lro/lro-l-lola-3-rdr-v1/lrolol_1xxx/data/lola_gdr/cylindrical/img/

Technologies

Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, SQLAlchemy), React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, Three.js (React Three Fiber), Recharts, Playwright.
